title: Abell 1689

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Arc-shaped objects curve around the galaxy cluster Abell 1689 in this Hubble image. They are galaxies located far behind the cluster, their light bent and stretched on the way to us.

The cluster contains a trillion stars, and their combined gravity acts like a zoom lens. Light from distant galaxies passing near the cluster is bent and magnified, an effect called gravitational lensing.

The magnification is the useful part. Because the lensed galaxies appear brighter and larger than they otherwise would, astronomers can study remote galaxies in far greater detail than they could without the cluster's help. In effect, the Universe has provided a natural telescope, and Hubble looks through it to see objects too faint to study on their own.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, red and near-infrared filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The faint lensed galaxies need Hubble's long exposures to appear, and part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see.
